chief_complaint: herald patch followed 2 weeks later by diffuse, mildly itchy oval salmon-colored plaques along Langer cleavage lines (Pityriasis Rosea)
hpi_details: 16F high school student presents with a rash that started 3 weeks ago as a single, 4 cm oval pinkish-tan patch on her lower back (`I thought it was ringworm and used antifungal cream without help`). Over the past week, suddenly developed dozens of smaller, mildly itchy, oval salmon-colored spots across her chest, back, and upper thighs. Perfectly healthy otherwise without fever, joint pain, or new medications.
ideas: thinks she caught severe widespread ringworm from gym class or an allergic reaction
concerns: embarrassed by rash covering her trunk and worried it will leave permanent scars on her body
expectations: wants strong prescription creams or pills to make the rash vanish quickly before prom next week

available_results.value: No fungal hyphae or spores seen

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pityriasis Rosea is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes reassurance that the rash is benign and self-limiting, with symptomatic relief via topical steroids and oral antihistamines for pruritus, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: herald patch followed 2 weeks later by diffuse, mildly itchy oval salmon-colored plaques along Langer cleavage lines (Pityriasis Rosea)

Key HPI features: 16F high school student presents with a rash that started 3 weeks ago as a single, 4 cm oval pinkish-tan patch on her lower back (`I thought it was ringworm and used antifungal cream without help`). Over the past week, suddenly developed dozens of smaller, mildly itchy, oval salmon-colored spots across her chest, back, and upper thighs. Perfectly healthy otherwise without fever, joint pain, or new medications.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 72, Temp 36.6C. Skin exam reveals a prominent 4 x 3 cm oval, fawn-colored plaque on the right lumbar back exhibiting a fine, collarette of scale oriented just inside the outer border (the primary 'Herald Patch'). Across the anterior and posterior trunk are multiple 1-2 cm discrete, oval, salmon-pink macules and thin plaques. On the back, the long axes of these oval lesions orient parallel to the skin cleavage lines (Langer lines), forming a striking, characteristic 'Christmas Tree' distribution pattern. Palms, soles, and mucous membranes are completely spared. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) skin scraping of the herald patch is completely negative for fungal hyphae/spores.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pityriasis Rosea.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Tinea corporis (the herald patch alone can mimic this) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Involvement of palms and soles — would suggest secondary syphilis instead, needing testing.
management_principles: Reassurance and education: explain that Pityriasis Rosea is a completely benign, self-limiting viral-reactive rash that is NOT contagious, NOT fungal, and will resolve completely without scarring over 6-8 weeks
Symptomatic relief: for mild pruritus, prescribe medium-potency topical steroid (Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% cream) and oral cetirizine
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Pityriasis Rosea (Self-limiting acute papulosquamous viral exanthem associated with HHV-6/HHV-7 reactivity).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Symptomatic relief: for mild pruritus, prescribe medium-potency topical steroid (Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% cream) and oral cetirizine. Avoid scrubbing or hot showers. Advise that no systemic antiviral or antibiotic therapy is required.

learning_objectives: Recognize the pathognomonic progression and morphology of Pityriasis Rosea (solitary 3-5 cm collarette-scaled Herald Patch followed 1-2 weeks later by secondary oval salmon plaques arranged along Langer lines in a 'Christmas Tree' pattern)
Perform bedside KOH prep to definitively exclude Tinea Corporis ('ringworm') when evaluating a Herald Patch

Differentiate Pityriasis Rosea from Secondary Syphilis (which typically involves the palms and soles, has generalized lymphadenopathy, and requires RPR/VDRL serology confirmation, especially in sexually active adolescents)
Provide empathetic patient reassurance regarding the benign, non-contagious, self-limiting 6-8 week natural history without unnecessary systemic medications

teaching.one_liner: A benign, self-limiting viral-reactive rash starting with a single 'herald patch' followed by a diffuse eruption of oval salmon-colored spots along the skin's natural cleavage lines — resolves on its own in 6-8 weeks.
differentials: Tinea corporis (the herald patch alone can mimic this)
red_flags: Involvement of palms and soles — would suggest secondary syphilis instead, needing testing

must_ask.say: Did this start with a single larger spot before the others appeared?
Are the spots mostly on your trunk, following a pattern like a Christmas tree?
Did you try an antifungal cream on the first spot, and did it help?
